It turned down the faith that Justinian's envoys brought. A chronicle written on the other side of the split says that Makuria too became Christian, around 569.

prose_changes.new: Christianity reached the Nubian kingdoms south of Egypt in the 540s, through two competing missions. A Miaphysite priest named Julian went with the empress Theodora's backing, and a Chalcedonian effort went with Justinian's. The story of that race survives only because a Syrian bishop, John of Ephesus, wrote it down from the winning side. What Nubia itself left is not stories but walls. Built a few generations later, the cathedral at Faras lay buried in sand until it was rescued before the Aswan dam flooded the region. It gave up a list of its bishops and more than a hundred painted figures: Nubian bishops, kings and queens, and saints. Some have dark faces and some pale, in a style nobody had seen before. When Arab armies pushed south after taking Egypt, Nubian archers held them at Dongola. In 652 the two sides signed the Baqt, a treaty of exchange rather than of conquest, and it left Christian Nubia standing on its own terms.

prose_changes.new: Aksum had been Christian since the fourth century. After Chalcedon it was a serious Red Sea power, with its own coinage and its own script, and its Bible was being translated into Ge'ez. Tradition credits the spread of monasticism and much of that translation work to the Nine Saints. They are said to have been monks from the Roman east, arriving around the turn of the sixth century. In 523 the Jewish king of Himyar, across the water in Yemen, massacred the Christians of Najran. The Aksumite king Kaleb crossed the Red Sea in about 525, killed him, and set up a Christian king who paid Aksum tribute. Not long after, the Aksumite soldiers who had stayed behind set up another king, Abramus, and Aksum could not remove him. A Miaphysite historian of the time counted the Aksumite king as a fellow believer. No text from inside these years shows where its church stood on Chalcedon. Evidence from these years is thin: inscriptions, a few very early gospel books, archaeology. Muslim tradition remembers that around 615 Muhammad sent his first followers to its king for protection.

This church left no successor. Latin Christianity in North Africa dwindled after the conquest and had all but disappeared by the later Middle Ages. It is the only major region of the ancient Christian world to vanish so completely. But it handed on its refusal. Its bishops wrote to the emperor to defend three sets of writings that they believed the council of Chalcedon had cleared. They would not condemn them. In 646 its councils wrote to Rome against the teaching of a single will in Christ. Their letters were read out at the Roman synod of 649, and the council of 680-681 later condemned that teaching. Its earlier centuries had already given the Latin church Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine. What this last century added was proof that a church in the provinces could tell an empire no. The ruins of Carthage and of dozens of African basilicas remain.

(1) 'Hardened a Western conviction that an emperor could not settle doctrine by decree': no vendored text shows that reception; restated as what Facundus (preface, to Justinian) and Victor of Tunnuna (s.a. 550) show. (2) 'Fed straight into the council of 680-681 that closed it': the vendored chain is the 646 letters read at the Lateran synod of 649 (Mansi X, lines 93425-93430) and Constantinople III's two-wills definition (NPNF 2.14, line 24884); restated as that sequence without the causal 'straight into'. The Three Chapters sentence says what the defenders believed, not that Chalcedon accepted all three: Theodoret and Ibas had been received there, Theodore had not (npnf214 22945-22946; Facundus, PL 67, 41877-41881).

prose_changes.new: Under Justinian, this church had no legal right to exist. Jacob Baradaeus was made its bishop when the Ghassanid Arab king Harith asked, and the empress Theodora backed it. For decades he crossed Syria and Mesopotamia, ordaining priests and bishops one step ahead of the bishops hunting him. When Byzantine power fell at Yarmouk in 636, its clergy stood on their own. They had never stopped their work, though for long years they had no legal standing at all.

This church is a direct heir of the Syriac Christian tradition. By the 550s a bishop appointed from Persia served at Kalyan, in western India. A traveler also reported a church on the pepper coast further south.

In 424 the bishops of the Persian Empire ruled that their catholicos at Seleucia-Ctesiphon answered to no bishop beyond their own frontier. This church lived under a Zoroastrian shah. It had taken the Nicene creed as its own in 410, but it would answer to no Roman bishop. Its answer to the question of Christ was not Chalcedon's, nor the Miaphysites'. It stood in the line of Theodore of Mopsuestia and held firmly that his divinity and his humanity were distinct. Its opponents fixed the name "Nestorian" on it. Its center of learning was the School of Nisibis. Written statutes there set out the students' day, their lodging and their discipline. Almost nothing else this early has left formation documents like them. Its communion reached far beyond Mesopotamia. In the 550s a traveler named Cosmas reported a bishop appointed from Persia at Kalyan, in western India. He also reported a church on the pepper coast further south. When the Sasanian empire fell to Arab armies by 651, the church carried straight on under new rulers and kept spreading east.

In the century after Chalcedon, monks settled in the ravines between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, and in the villages around Gaza. They became almost a second population. In the laurae, hermits lived apart through the week and gathered on Sundays. Shared houses held hundreds. This tradition stands out clearly because its own papers survive. Cyril of Scythopolis wrote carefully dated lives of Euthymius, Sabas and the men who came after them. Two recluses near Gaza, Barsanuphius and John, left roughly 850 letters. They answered monks, married couples, sick people and local officials, one question at a time. Most of the Judean houses came to back Chalcedon. Euthymius took the council's side. His biographer says nearly all the desert monks would have followed him, had a rival monk named Theodosius not turned many of them against it. Near Gaza, Peter the Iberian became bishop for those who rejected the council. The empire pulled the monks hard into its fights over doctrine. One was the purge of teaching drawn from Origen in the 550s, which split their own houses. In 614 the Persian army sacked Jerusalem and tore through the desert houses. Those who lived wrote down what was lost.

prose_changes.new: The kingdom of Kartli, in what is now eastern Georgia, became Christian in the fourth century. It came through the preaching of a woman the tradition calls Nino. Kartli then held on to that faith for three centuries, on a frontier where Persia had every reason to prise it loose. Its oldest surviving book, written in the 470s or 480s, tells the story of Shushanik. She was an Armenian princess married to the local ruler. He left Christianity for Zoroastrianism, and when she would not follow him, he locked her up and beat her until she died. Georgia built its own alphabet, its own monasteries, and an unusually rich life of worship. Georgian manuscripts keep the worship of fifth- to eighth-century Jerusalem more fully than any Greek source does. Around 600, at the third council of Dvin, its church broke with Armenia and took the Chalcedonian side. That is why the two neighboring churches of the Caucasus have belonged to different communions ever since.

prose_changes.new: Beside Armenia and Georgia there was a third Christian kingdom in the Caucasus. This was Albania, in what is now Azerbaijan and the south of Dagestan. It had its own royal line, its own bishops and its own alphabet. In the late fifth century it held a council at Aghuen. The council made rules for the clergy and for marriage, and set out what the nobles owed the church. Albania also produced a history, put together from older material by a writer known as Movses Daskhurantsi. That is very nearly all the story it left. It was pressed between Persian, Byzantine and then Arab power, and between the rival loyalties of its Armenian and Georgian neighbors. In the early 700s it lost its independent standing, when its catholicos was placed under the Armenian church. Its written language was all but lost for more than a thousand years. Then, in 1996, palimpsests at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Sinai were found to hold Caucasian Albanian scripture. The pages had been scraped and written over with later Georgian text.

prose_changes.new: Gregory was a monk and wrote the only life of Benedict there is. But his own work was a bishop's: the Pastoral Rule is a manual for bishops, and the Register is the paperwork of a government. His letters also tell us about the early English church, the Frankish church of Gaul and the imperial church at Constantinople.

prose_changes.new: The Pastoral Rule became the standard book on the bishop's office in the West, and it stayed in use for a thousand years. Carolingian councils told all bishops to study it. Hincmar of Rheims reports that new bishops were handed a copy at their consecration. Alfred had it translated into English, meaning, he said, to send a copy to every bishop in his kingdom. The mission to Kent is why there is an English church in communion with Rome at all. It is also why the early English church has a Roman half. Then there is the working model of the bishop of Rome as the practical government of central Italy. He fed the city from church estates, dealt with invaders and paid troops. That is where the temporal power of the papacy really begins, whatever later documents claimed for it.

The Carolingian sentence now matches Barmby (npnf212 24040-24058): councils of 813 and 836 enjoined study of the book; handing a copy to new bishops was a custom Hincmar reports, not a council ruling.
